title: When does a drawn human figure look like a real person?
description: A friend's head, torso, arms and legs are measured and then drawn smaller. The video multiplies all four lengths by one factor, then tries one length with a different factor and checks each length by dividing new by old.
teaching_notes: One idea: a drawing looks real when every length is scaled by the same factor. Watch for students who scale only some of the lengths and wonder why the figure looks odd.

source: Figure it Out (ratios and proportions, question 7)
video_script.why: The child carries the factor test from pictures to a drawn body, and sees why one length scaled differently spoils the figure.
video_script.substitution: Multiply the head, torso, arms and legs by one factor, then divide new by old for each length to check.
video_script.anchor: a friend's body measured in four lengths: head, torso, arms and legs
video_script.payoff_line: When every length changes by the same factor, the figure looks realistic.

final_answer.spoken: yes, the figure looks realistic when every length changes by the same factor

hold_back: Answer: yes, it looks more realistic
maths_rules: sample measures used to show the method (the book asks the child to measure a friend): head 20 cm, torso 60 cm, arms 60 cm, legs 80 cm
factor 1/10: 20 × 1/10 = 2; 60 × 1/10 = 6; 60 × 1/10 = 6; 80 × 1/10 = 8; so the drawing is head 2 cm, torso 6 cm, arms 6 cm, legs 8 cm
one length with another factor: legs drawn 4 cm; 4 ÷ 80 = 1/20, which is not 1/10, so the legs look too short
video_script.design: One idea: one factor on every length gives a realistic figure. Uses the factor of change from the solved example. The measured body stays for the whole video.
open_questions: The book asks the child to measure a friend, so the video shows the method on sample measures: head 20 cm, torso 60 cm, arms 60 cm, legs 80 cm.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about drawing human figures.
<bookmark mark='body'/>You measure a friend's head, torso, arms and legs, and then draw a smaller figure.
<bookmark mark='len'/>Say the head is twenty, the torso and arms are sixty, and the legs are eighty.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Will the drawing look more real if every length is scaled the same way?

beats.on_screen: the figure and the empty page hold still and the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the tiger picture from before beside the figure; one factor tag joins each old length to a new length; the tiger's width and height tags match

marks.tiger: the tiger picture appears with its width and height tags matching
marks.body: four arrows join the four body lengths to four new lengths
marks.one: one factor is written on all four arrows

narration: <bookmark mark='tiger'/>A tiger picture looks right when its width and height change by one factor.
<bookmark mark='body'/>We use the same way as the example in your book, but now with four lengths.
<bookmark mark='one'/>Pick one factor and multiply the head, torso, arms and legs by it.

beats.on_screen: Given: head 20 cm, torso 60 cm, arms 60 cm, legs 80 cm

marks.given: the four lengths are written one under the other

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the head is twenty and the torso is sixty. The arms are sixty and the legs are eighty centimetres.

beats.on_screen: To find: the drawn lengths, and whether the figure looks real

marks.find: the words to find are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the drawn lengths, and see whether the figure looks real.

marks.head: 20 × 1/10 = 2 is written
marks.legs: 80 × 1/10 = 8 is written, and a small figure is drawn with these lengths

narration: <bookmark mark='f'/>Step one, multiply every length by the factor one tenth.
<bookmark mark='head'/>Twenty times one tenth is two.
<bookmark mark='torso'/>Sixty times one tenth is six, for the torso and for the arms.
<bookmark mark='arms'/>Eighty times one tenth is eight, for the legs.
<bookmark mark='legs'/>We draw a figure with head two, torso six, arms six, and legs eight.

beats.on_screen: Legs drawn 4 cm instead: 4 ÷ 80 = 1/20, not 1/10; the legs look too short

marks.alt: a second figure appears with legs of 4 cm
marks.warn: 1/20 shows in the warning colour next to 1/10

narration: <bookmark mark='alt'/>Step two, try drawing the legs only four centimetres long.
<bookmark mark='f'/>Four divided by eighty is one twentieth.
<bookmark mark='warn'/>That is not one tenth, so the legs look too short for the rest of the body.

marks.chk: the words Check: new ÷ old are written
marks.four: 2 ÷ 20, 6 ÷ 60, 6 ÷ 60 and 8 ÷ 80 are written, each equal to 1/10
marks.tick: a tick lands on all four factors

narration: <bookmark mark='chk'/>Step three, divide each new length by the old length to check.
<bookmark mark='four'/>Two divided by twenty is one tenth, and so is six divided by sixty. Eight divided by eighty is also one tenth.
<bookmark mark='tick'/>All four lengths have the same factor.

beats.on_screen: Answer: yes, it looks more realistic when all four lengths change by the same factor
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>When every length changes by the same factor, the figure looks realistic.
